The Crucifix sea catfish, Sciades proops, attains a maximum total length of 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger ariid species inhabiting estuarine and coastal waters of the western Atlantic. Populations sampled in the Maranhão region of Brazil exhibit a total length at puberty of 36.6 centimeters [Lp = 36.6 centimeters], a value that is notably lower than the standard length of 51.1 centimeters reported for this species in earlier work by Lecomte and Meunier. This discrepancy likely reflects methodological differences in morphometric measurement conventions between studies, as total length consistently exceeds standard length due to the inclusion of the caudal fin. The attainment of sexual maturity at a relatively modest body length suggests that Sciades proops follows a life-history strategy characterized by early reproductive onset, a pattern observed in several other ariid catfishes that inhabit seasonally variable environments where early breeding confers a selective advantage. Such a strategy may be linked to the energetic demands of oral incubation, a reproductive mode that imposes significant constraints on the size and condition of breeding individuals.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of female Sciades proops reaches a mean value of 15% [GSI = 15%] at 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C]. Field collections conducted during the peak reproductive months indicate that the wet weight at puberty for females is approximately 545 grams [Wwp = approximately 545 grams], a mass that is reached after approximately 730 days after birth [tp = approximately 730 days after birth], a relatively rapid developmental trajectory for a fish of this ultimate body size. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a power-law function derived from a large sample of individuals across the size range, providing a reliable basis for estimating body condition and reproductive status from field measurements. These reproductive metrics are essential for parameterizing population models aimed at assessing the sustainability of artisanal fisheries that target this species in northeastern Brazil.

Neonatal mass in Sciades proops has been estimated at 2.14 grams [Wwb = 2.14 grams] based on the typical egg diameter of 16 millimeters observed in congeneric species within the genus Sciades. Although direct measurements of newly emerged larvae are scarce due to the difficulty of sampling during the oral incubation period, the relationship between egg size and hatchling mass is well established among ariid catfishes, which produce relatively large, yolk-rich eggs compared to many other teleost families. The large egg diameter, corresponding to an approximate spherical volume of 2.14 cubic centimeters, yields a substantial yolk reserve that supports an extended lecithotrophic phase during which the yolk-sac larva remains nutritionally independent. This period of endogenous nutrition is critical for the survival of offspring in the turbid, organically rich estuarine environments where this species typically spawns, as it allows larvae to develop functional feeding structures before they must rely on exogenous prey. The substantial investment in individual offspring is consistent with the low fecundity characteristic of mouthbrooding catfishes.

Within the family Ariidae, Sciades proops is notable for its large ultimate body size: the maximum recorded wet weight is 9,000 grams [Wwi = 9,000 grams], a value documented in published fisheries surveys from the Amazon delta and adjacent coastal regions. This asymptotic body mass is achieved only by the oldest and largest specimens, which typically correspond to females that have accumulated considerable somatic reserves over a prolonged growth period. Body mass shows pronounced variation with latitude and local environmental conditions, with individuals from more productive estuarine systems attaining larger sizes than those from oligotrophic waters. The length-weight relationship for this species indicates that mass increases approximately as the cube of length, consistent with isometric growth in body shape throughout the juvenile and adult stages. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Sciades herzbergii reveal that Sciades proops attains a substantially greater maximum mass, suggesting fundamental differences in life-history allocation patterns between these closely related taxa that share similar geographic ranges.

Longevity in Sciades proops has been estimated at 1,460 days [am = 1,460 days] at 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], corresponding to approximately four years of natural lifespan in wild populations. This estimate is derived from mark-recapture studies and analysis of otolith annuli, which reveal a relatively rapid life cycle for a fish of this maximum body mass. The four-year lifespan is consistent with the species' early maturation and high reproductive investment, traits that collectively define a life-history strategy oriented toward rapid population turnover in dynamic coastal environments. This rapid initial growth allows females to attain reproductive size quickly, after which somatic growth decelerates markedly, with the maximum mass of 9,000 grams reached only near the end of the four-year lifespan. The senescence phase appears to be brief, with most individuals exhibiting a sharp decline in body condition during the third and fourth years, followed by natural mortality.
